summary.method: Five Claude agents each took two chapters, read an index of all 1,330 readings, and proposed up to 3 links per verse after reading the Tamil and commentaries of both verses. Existing links were hidden from them. Five other agents graded the proposals blind, mixed with 40 unmarked links whose grades were known.
summary.recall: 45 of the 73 known sound links touching these chapters were proposed again
summary.coverage: Pilot verses with a sound link rose from 55 to 99 of 100
summary.limits: All proposers and graders are Claude without a Tamil lexicon. The proposals have longer, more careful notes than the earlier links, and graders judge the link as written, so a persuasive note may raise a grade: 10 pairs earlier graded weak were graded sound with the new note. No Tamil scholar has reviewed any of this.

links.note: Verse 1 says the world has ஆதி பகவன் as its first (முதற்றே உலகு), as letters have அ. Verse 543 uses the same word for the king's sceptre: it stands as the ஆதி of the antaṇar's books and of aram (அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as their cause (காரணம்). The pairing shows the book giving the world one 'first' in its opening and giving aram itself a second, political one in Book 2.
links.reason: The word ஆதி occurs in 'ஆதி பகவன் முதற்றே உலகு' and in 'அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்'; the sceptre as the 'first' of aram set beside the world's 'first' is a meaningful reuse and the note's gloss report is accurate.

links.note: Verse 1 names a first of the world (ஆதி பகவன் முதற்றே உலகு) and the chapter goes on to ask for reverence. Verse 1062 is the one place that speaks of a maker of the world (உலகியற்றியான்), and it wishes him to wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக) if he requires that some live by begging. Read together, the figure at the head of the world is praised in one place and held answerable in the other; whether the two are the same figure is an inference, since verse 1 says 'first', not 'maker'.
links.reason: The two verses share no image or word ('ஆதி பகவன் முதற்றே' against 'உலகியற்றியான்'), and the note itself admits that the identity of the two figures is an inference. The contrast of reverence and conditional curse ('பரந்து கெடுக') is worth noting, but it does not fit same_image or cleanly fit any other type.

links.note: Verse 2 denies any fruit to learning without worship. Verse 140 says those who have not learned to live in accord with the world are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும் கல்லார் அறிவிலாதார்). The same discounting of book-learning recurs with a social test in place of a devotional one.
links.reason: 'கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்' and 'பலகற்றும் கல்லார் அறிவிலாதார்' both discount learning that fails an external test (worship / 'உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்').

links.note: Verse 2: what has learning yielded, if one does not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்)? Verse 315: does understanding achieve anything (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own? Both are rhetorical questions that judge knowledge by a test outside knowledge, worship in one and compassion in the other.
links.reason: Both are rhetorical questions on the yield of knowing ('கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்' / 'அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ') conditioned on a test outside knowledge (தொழாஅர் எனின் / போற்றாக் கடை).

links.note: Verse 2 asks what use learning is (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயன் என்கொல்) if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge. Verse 356 states the fruit positively: those who learn here and see the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not returning. Parimelazhagar reads verse 2's fruit as ending rebirth too, so 356 spells out what verse 2 leaves as a question.
links.reason: கற்றதனால் ஆய பயன் என்கொல் is answered by கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் தலைப்படுவர் மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி: learning's fruit is stated positively. The reading of Parimelazhagar on verse 2 fits his usual gloss.

links.note: Verses 3 and 6 end on the same words, நீடுவாழ்வார், 'will live long'. Verse 3 gives this to those who reach the feet (மாணடி சேர்ந்தார்); verse 6 gives it to those who stand in the path of conduct free of falsehood (பொய்தீர் ஒழுக்க நெறி நின்றார்) of the one who quenched the five. The repeated ending puts devotion and conduct side by side as routes to the same result.
links.reason: Both end நீடுவாழ்வார், given once to மாணடி சேர்ந்தார் and once to பொய்தீர் ஒழுக்க நெறி நின்றார். The repeated close is distinctive and the note reads both lines correctly, though it is a modest point within one chapter.

links.note: Verse 4 describes the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no affliction. Verse 350 turns the same description into an instruction: hold to the hold of the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), in order to let attachment go (பற்று விடற்கு). Parimelazhagar notes that பற்றற்றான் is chosen to match the invocation chapter; 350 supplies the mechanism verse 4 leaves unstated.
links.reason: வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான் and பற்றற்றான் describe the same figure, and 350 makes holding to him the means (பற்று விடற்கு). Parimelazhagar does say கடவுள் வாழ்த்திற்கு ஏற்ப ... 'பற்றற்றான்' என்றார், as cited.

links.note: Both verses turn on the word வேண்டாமை but use it differently. In verse 4 it is paired with வேண்டுதல் as something the Lord lacks, which Parimelazhagar glosses as aversion (வெறுத்தல்). In 362 வேண்டாமை is desirelessness, the thing to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்) so that birthlessness comes. A reader should not carry one sense into the other.
links.reason: வேண்டாமை does occur in both and the two senses are described correctly (aversion beside வேண்டுதல் in 4; desirelessness in 362), but the note's point is that the uses are unrelated, so the link is a lexical caution rather than a meaningful shared image.

links.note: Verse 4 says there is no இடும்பை at any time for those who reach the feet of the one free of liking and aversion. Verse 628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure and calls இடும்பை natural (இன்பம் விழையான் இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்) does not come to pain. The Book 2 verse keeps the link between absent desire and absent suffering but drops the devotional route, and it concedes that the affliction itself still arrives.
links.reason: Both tie absence of wanting to absence of இடும்பை/துன்பம் ('வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான் ... இடும்பை இல'; 'இன்பம் விழையான் ... துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்'), and 628's 'இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்' does concede that affliction arrives. In 4 the desirelessness belongs to the deity, not the devotee, which the note blurs slightly but does not misstate.

links.note: Verse 5 says both kinds of deed, which belong to darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும்), do not attach to those who dwell on the Lord's praise; Parimelazhagar explains that good deeds too are a cause of birth. Verse 38 says that doing good (நன்றாற்றின்) with no day lost is the stone that blocks the road of one's days, which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as ending rebirth. On those readings one verse counts good deeds among what binds and the other makes them what frees.
links.reason: On Parimelazhagar's reading 'இருவினையும்' in 5 includes நல்வினை as a cause of birth, while 38's 'நன்றாற்றின் ... வாழ்நாள் வழியடைக்கும் கல்' makes doing good what stops rebirth (both commentators); the note names the readings the conflict depends on.

links.note: Verse 5 ties the two kinds of deed to இருள், which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss as delusion. Verse 352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left confusion (மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு), darkness goes and joy comes (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும்). The later verse gives knowledge as what removes the darkness that verse 5 only names.
links.reason: 'இருள்சேர் இருவினை' and 'இருள்நீங்கி ... மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு' share இருள், and 352 does give clear sight as what removes it. The note should have said this fits Manakkudavar ('அறியாமையாகிய இருள்'); Parimelazhagar takes இருள் in 352 as hell standing for birth.

links.note: Verse 5 speaks of the praise of இறைவன், the chapter's word for the Lord. Verse 388 says a king who does justice and protects is set down as இறை for the people (மக்கட்கு இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). The shared word shows that the title used for the deity in chapter 1 is one a human ruler earns by conduct in Book 2.
links.reason: இறைவன் in 5 and மக்கட்கு இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும் in 388 share the title, and 388 plainly makes it something a king earns by முறைசெய்து காப்பாற்றும். The shared word is meaningful, not incidental.

links.note: Verse 6 calls the deity பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான், the one who quenched the five of the sense-gates. Verse 25 uses the same ஐந்தவித்தான் for the human renouncer, whose strength Indra is witness to. The epithet is not reserved for the divine: the book's ascetic ideal and its deity are described in the same word.
links.reason: The identical epithet 'ஐந்தவித்தான்' is used of the deity in 6 ('பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்') and of the human renouncer in 25 ('ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல்'); a distinctive shared word with a real point.

links.note: Verse 6 promises long life to those who stand in the path of the one who quenched the five. Verse 126 gives the human practice and its reward: if one can draw in the five like a tortoise in one birth (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), it is a protection for seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Verse 126 says அடக்கல், holding in, where verse 6 says அவித்தான், quenched, so the follower's task is stated more modestly than the exemplar's.
links.reason: ஐந்தவித்தான் and ஐந்தடக்கல் are the same five, with a reward attached in both (நீடுவாழ்வார்; எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). The அவித்தல்/அடக்கல் contrast is the note's inference but is fairly drawn from the words.

links.note: Verse 7 says it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety (மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது) except for those who reach the feet of the one without equal. Verse 622 says a flood of affliction perishes when a person of understanding thinks in his own mind (அறிவுடையான் உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்). The conflict holds if மனக்கவலை is ordinary mental distress, as Manakkudavar's gloss allows; Parimelazhagar narrows it to the sufferings of rebirth, which 622 does not address.
links.reason: 7: மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது except for தாள்சேர்ந்தார்; 622: இடும்பை ... அறிவுடையான் உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும். A real conflict if கவலை is ordinary distress, and the note names the reading it depends on.

links.note: Verse 7 makes freedom from mental anxiety rare, reserved for those who reach the Lord's feet. Verse 1072 says, with irony, that the base are better off than those who know the good, because they have no distress in their hearts (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). Read beside verse 7 it marks that mere absence of worry is not the state the invocation is praising, since the base have it too.
links.reason: மனக்கவலை and நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் do meet, but 1072 is an ironic jab at the கயவர், not a limit on verse 7; the 'counterfeit calm' lesson is the note's construction rather than something either verse states.

links.note: Verse 8 calls the deity அறவாழி அந்தணன், joining அந்தணன் to aram. Verse 30 defines the word: those called அந்தணர் are the people of aram (அறவோர்), because they act with kindness toward every living being (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Verse 30 gives the reason for the pairing of title and virtue that verse 8 assumes.
links.reason: 8 joins the two words in 'அறவாழி அந்தணன்' and 30 defines the title by the virtue: 'அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர் ... செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்'. The note is accurate.

links.note: Verse 8 uses ஆழி for the deity (அறவாழி), read as 'sea of aram' by Parimelazhagar, who also records the reading 'wheel of aram'. Verse 989 calls the worthy சான்றாண்மைக்கு ஆழி and says they do not shift even if the age shifts; there Parimelazhagar reads ஆழி as the shore of the sea of worth. The same word is attached to a virtue in both verses, to a god in one and to people in the other, and its sense is disputed in both.
links.reason: The word ஆழி attaches to a virtue in both ('அறவாழி', 'சான்றாண்மைக்கு ஆழி'), and the commentary reports are accurate, but on the readings given it means sea in one and shore in the other; as written the link is a shared, disputed word more than a shared image.

links.note: Verse 8 says the other seas are hard to swim (பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது) except for those who reach the feet of the antaṇan who is a sea of aram; Parimelazhagar takes the other seas to be wealth and pleasure and the feet to be the raft. In 1164 the woman says the sea of kāmam is there and the safe raft to swim it is not (காமக் கடல் ... அதுநீந்தும் ஏமப் புணை ... இல்). Book 3 shows from inside one of the seas that Parimelazhagar finds in verse 8, with the raft named and missing.
links.reason: 'பிறவாழி நீந்தல்' and 'காமக் கடல் ... நீந்தும் ஏமப் புணை' share the swim-the-sea figure; Parimelazhagar does gloss the feet as 'தாள் ஆகிய புணை' and the other seas as பொருள் and இன்பம், so the note is accurate.

links.note: Verse 9 treats a sense organ that does not grasp (கோளில் பொறி) as the type of uselessness, while verse 6 praises the one who quenched the five of the sense-gates (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்). Parimelazhagar reads what is quenched in verse 6 as the five desires that travel by the senses, not the senses. Taken together the two verses of the chapter support that reading: a dead sense is a defect, and what is praised is something else.
links.reason: 'கோளில் பொறி' as the type of uselessness beside 'பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்' does support Parimelazhagar's gloss that what is quenched is the five desires, not the organs; the note is accurate and hedged.

links.note: Verse 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is without worth, like a sense organ that does not grasp (கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே). Verse 418 says ears not pierced by listening are of a deaf kind even though they hear (கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே). Both measure a part of the body by one proper use and call it dead without that use; the use is worship in one and learning by ear in the other.
links.reason: வணங்காத் தலை is like கோளில் பொறி; செவி not தோட்கப்பட்ட by கேள்வி is கேளாத் தகைய. Both judge an organ by its proper use; worship in one, learning in the other.

links.note: Verse 9 compares the unbowing head to an organ that is present and does not sense. Verse 574 asks what eyes without kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து எவன் செய்யும்). The figure of the organ that is there and useless is applied in Book 2 to a ruler's compassion.
links.reason: 'கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே' and 'உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்' use the same figure of an organ that is present and does nothing, in devotion and in rule.

links.note: Verses 8 and 10 both speak of swimming a sea with the Lord's feet as the condition. Verse 10 names the sea as birth (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்); verse 8 says only 'the other seas' (பிறவாழி), which Parimelazhagar takes as wealth and pleasure. On his reading the chapter has two different seas; without it, verse 8 can look like a first statement of verse 10.
links.reason: 'பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்' and 'பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது', each conditioned on reaching the feet (அடி/தாள் சேர்); the note correctly flags that the sea of 8 is unnamed and reading-dependent.

links.note: Verse 10 makes reaching the Lord's feet the condition for crossing birth: those who do not reach them do not swim it (நீந்தார் இறைவனடி சேராதார்). Verse 349 gives a condition with no deity in it: the moment attachment is cut, that cuts birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). The next verse, 350, joins the two by telling one to hold to the one without attachment in order to drop attachment, so 349 shows what reaching the feet has to accomplish.
links.reason: The connection is real ('இறைவன் அடிசேராதார் நீந்தார்' against 'பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்', bridged by 350), but 349 neither limits 10 nor adds a condition to it; it supplies the mechanism, which is a development. The closing claim about 'what reaching the feet has to accomplish' is the note's inference, leaning on 350.

links.note: Verse 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of birth and others do not. In 1167 the woman says she swims the fierce flood of kāmam and sees no shore (நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்), alone even at midnight. The swimmer who cannot cross, stated as doctrine in verse 10, is spoken in the first person in Book 3.
links.reason: 'பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் நீந்தார்' and 'காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்' share the figure of a swimmer in a water that cannot be crossed, as doctrine and as first-person lament.

links.note: Verse 31 says aram yields wealth and asks what greater gain a living being has. Verse 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are to be thought about (நினைக்கப்படும்). Parimelazhagar says such outcomes cannot come from crookedness or uprightness and sends the wise to look for a cause in past deeds; either way 169 limits how far verse 31 can be read as a promise visible in one life. His gloss on 31 itself takes செல்வம் as heavenly goods.
links.reason: சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும் is checked by 169's admission that அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான் கேடும் occur and must be நினைக்கப்படும். The note's account of Parimelazhagar on both verses is accurate.

links.note: Verse 31 says aram yields distinction and yields wealth too (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Verse 754 uses the same construction with the terms turned round: wealth that came by known means and without wrong yields aram and yields pleasure too (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). Book 1 has virtue producing wealth and Book 2 has rightly earned wealth producing virtue, in matching words.
links.reason: சிறப்பீனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும் (of அறம்) and அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் (of தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்) mirror each other in construction with the terms reversed.

links.note: Verse 32 says no ruin (கேடு) surpasses forgetting aram. Verse 117 gives the other side: the world will not count as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays fair and rests in the good. Together they define ruin by one's relation to virtue and not by one's circumstances.

links.note: Verse 32 says there is no gain beyond aram (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை). Verse 122 says of restraint that a living being has no gain beyond it (ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு), in nearly the same words as verses 31 and 32. The repeated formula shows that 'nothing surpasses this' is a way the book commends a virtue, and that restraint is being placed inside aram, not set against it.
links.reason: அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை and ஆக்கம் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு are the same formula, as is 31's ஆக்கம் எவனோ உயிர்க்கு. The formula point is right; 'restraint placed inside aram' is a mild extra inference.

links.note: Verse 32 names forgetting (மறத்தல்) of aram as the greatest ruin. In the chapter on heedlessness, 532 says forgetfulness kills renown (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை) as unrelieved poverty kills understanding. The idea that the damage comes through lapse of attention, without any act of wrongdoing, is carried from ethics into statecraft.
links.reason: 'அதனை மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு' and 'பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை' both locate ruin in forgetting or heedlessness rather than in a positive wrong, in ethics and in statecraft.

links.note: Verse 33 asks for aram everywhere and without a break (ஓவாதே ... எல்லாம் செயல்). Verse 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, then not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 297, that it is better to hold one virtue unfailingly than to take on many and fail in some, this is advice to narrow what verse 33 tells one to spread as widely as possible.

links.note: Verse 33 limits its command with ஒல்லும் வகையான், 'in the way that is possible'. Parimelazhagar explains this for the householder as acting in proportion to one's means, and 477 says so directly: give knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து ஈக), for that is the way to guard wealth while giving. Verse 477 gives the practical content of the qualifier in verse 33. This edition prints அறவறிந்து in 477; the commentary reads அளவு அறிந்து.

links.note: Verse 33 says to do the work of aram by whatever means one can (ஒல்லும் வகையான்), without ceasing, wherever it can go (செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் செயல்). Verse 673, on how to carry out a task, uses the same words: where it is possible the deed is good, and where it is not, act looking for a way that goes (ஒல்லும்வாய் ... செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்). The rule for virtue and the rule for state action are built from the same vocabulary of the possible. This edition prints the first word of 673 as ஙல்லும், a typo for ஒல்லும், as its own commentary shows.

links.note: Verse 34 says being without stain in the mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is the whole of aram and the rest is noise (ஆகுல நீர). Verse 278 shows the rest in practice: many, with the stain in their minds (மனத்தது மாசாக), bathe as though they were great and live concealed. The chapter on false conduct supplies the case that verse 34 dismisses in general terms.
links.reason: மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் versus மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி: 278 is the concrete case of the ஆகுல நீர that 34 dismisses.

links.note: Verse 34 sets inner cleanness against outward show. Verse 298 makes the same division and adds how the inner kind is known: outer purity is had by water, and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). It gives a test for the state that verse 34 only asserts. This edition prints புறள்தூய்மை for புறந்தூய்மை.
links.reason: மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் in 34 and அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும் in 298 share the inner/outer split, and 298 adds how inner purity is known. Note is accurate.

links.note: Verse 34 places all of aram in a stainless mind. Verse 455 says purity of mind and purity of action both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). If so, the inner state verse 34 treats as the whole matter depends on something outside the person.

links.note: Verse 35 lists envy (அழுக்காறு) first among what aram must avoid. Verse 161 turns that item into a positive rule: take as your way of conduct (ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க) a nature that has no envy in the heart. The chapter on envy opens by treating as a discipline what verse 35 states as an exclusion.

links.note: Verse 35 defines aram as what goes on without slipping into four things: envy, craving, anger and harsh speech (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). Verse 360 gives a shorter list for the renouncer: when even the names of desire, anger and confusion (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்) are gone, pain goes. Anger and desire appear in both; the householder's list adds faults that touch other people, and the renouncer's adds the confusion at their root. The edition's Tamil for 360 is misprinted (இநவ்முன்றன் for இவை மூன்றன்).
links.reason: 'அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்' and 'காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்' overlap in desire and anger (வெகுளி verbatim), and the note's contrast of the householder's and renouncer's lists is fair.
links.text_issue: 360 is misprinted 'இநவ்முன்றன்' for 'இவை மூன்றன்', as the note says.

links.note: Verse 35 defines aram by the absence of four faults. Verse 431 defines a sound prosperity the same way for a ruler: the increase of those without arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்) has dignity. Anger is on both lists; Parimelazhagar glosses சிறுமை in 431 as lust, which would bring the two lists closer still.
links.reason: Both define by absent faults and share anger ('வெகுளி' / 'சினம்'), but lists of faults are common in the book and the other items do not match. Parimelazhagar's 'காமம்' for சிறுமை is not the same as 35's 'அவா'.

links.note: Verse 36 calls aram a companion that does not perish (பொன்றாத் துணை). Verse 233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands unperishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்), using the same word. Read literally the second excludes the first. Parimelazhagar's reading of 36, that the merit goes with the soul into another body, puts it outside 'the world' of 233; Kalaignar reads 36 itself as lasting fame, which removes the conflict another way.

links.note: Verse 36 says to do aram without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது), because it is the companion that does not perish when one perishes. The later verse shows the moment that verse 36 calls பொன்றுங்கால்.

links.note: Verse 36 says aram done now stays as a companion at death. Verse 398 says the learning one has acquired in one birth is a protection through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both speak of something gained in this life that is not lost with the body; Book 2 says of learning what Book 1 says of virtue.

links.note: On the reading of Parimelazhagar and Pope, verse 37 explains the difference between palanquin rider and bearer by aram done before. Verse 270 reasons the same way about a whole society: the reason the have-nots are many is that those who do tavam are few and those who do not are many. Both read present inequality as the result of past practice; Parimelazhagar adds that wealth and want in 270 also mean understanding and its lack.

links.note: Verse 37 says there is no need to state the way of aram: look between the one who carries the palanquin and the one who rides (பொறுத்தானொடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை). Parimelazhagar and Pope take this to mean that the fruit of virtue can be seen in who rides and who carries. Verse 973 says those who are not high are not high even when seated high (மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர்), and Parimelazhagar reads the seating there as wealth and poverty. On those readings one verse lets position show merit and the other denies that position shows anything about the person. The Tamil of 37 is elliptical and does not itself say which of the two is the virtuous one.

links.note: Verse 38 says daily good is a stone that shuts the road of one's வாழ்நாள்; Parimelazhagar takes வாழ்நாள் as the days of living in a body, so that shutting the road means no more births. Verse 326 says Death does not advance on the வாழ்நாள் of one who keeps to not killing. On Parimelazhagar's reading the same word names something virtue ends in 38 and something virtue protects in 326. On Kalaignar's reading of 38, where the stone smooths life's road, there is no conflict.

links.note: Verse 38 treats each day as something that can fall away unused or be filled with good. Verse 334 says what a day is: it shows itself as one thing called a day, and it is a blade sawing through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. Verse 334 gives the reason for the daily urgency of verse 38.

links.note: Verse 38 speaks of doing good so that no day falls away unused (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை). In 776 the warrior takes up his days and sets among the lapsed all those on which he took no honourable wound (விழுப்புண் படாதநாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள் வைக்கும்). Both keep an account of days and call a day lost by one standard, good done in one and wounds borne in the other.
links.reason: 'வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை' and 'விழுப்புண் படாதநாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள் வைக்கும்' both audit one's days and count a day lost by a single standard, in ethics and in war.

links.note: Verse 39 says only what comes by aram is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and the rest lies outside and has no renown either. Verse 156 allows that those who retaliate do get joy, for one day (ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம்), while those who forbear have renown for as long as things last (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்; until the world perishes, in Parimelazhagar's gloss). It keeps verse 39's pairing of joy and renown but concedes a short pleasure outside virtue, so the 'only' of 39 reads as a judgment of worth and not a denial that such pleasure is felt.
links.reason: 39's exclusive 'அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம் ... புகழும் இல' meets 156's concession 'ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம்' with புகழ் reserved for the forbearing; the same joy/renown pair, and a real qualification of the 'only'.

links.note: Verse 39 divides joy into what comes by aram and everything else. Verse 173 names the two sides: those who want the other joy (மற்றின்பம்) will not do what is not aram out of desire for a small joy (சிற்றின்பம்). Parimelazhagar glosses the small joy as the unstable pleasure got from goods taken from others, and the other joy as the stable joy that comes by aram (அறத்தான் வரும் நிலையுடைய இன்பம்), which is the wording of verse 39. Verse 173 thus applies 39's division to a single temptation.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar glosses 173's 'மற்றின்பம்' as 'அறத்தான் வரும் நிலையுடைய இன்பம்', the wording of 39 ('அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்'), and 'சிற்றின்பம்' as the unstable joy of taken goods; 173 applies 39's division to coveting.

links.note: Verse 40 names blame (பழி) as the thing to escape. Verse 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one gives up what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). Both make avoidance of the blameworthy the working test, verse 280 applying it to the ascetic in place of outward marks.
links.reason: 'உயற்பாலது … பழி' and 'உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்' both make avoiding the blamed the operative test, 280 against outward marks (மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும்).

links.note: Verse 40 gives a two-sided rule: what one should do is aram, and what one should escape is blame (செயற்பாலது ... அறனே, உயற்பாலது ... பழி). Verse 466 gives the same two sides to a ruler as consequences: one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and ruined also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Book 2 restates the pair as policy and makes the omission as costly as the wrong act.
links.reason: 'செயற்பாலது … உயற்பாலது' and 'செய்தக்க அல்ல செய / செய்தக்க செய்யாமை' share the gerundive two-sided frame; 466 recasts it prudentially (கெடும்) and adds omission. A little loose, since 40's second half is blame to avoid, not an omission.

links.note: Verse 40 says blame is what a person should escape. Verse 656 tests that rule at its hardest: even if one must see the hunger of the mother who bore one, do not do the deed the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை). It shows that the avoidance of blame in verse 40 is meant to hold against a competing duty, and it names whose blame counts.
links.reason: 40's 'உயற்பால தோரும் பழி' is tested by 656's 'ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும்' and specified as 'சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை'; a real application of the rule to a hard case.

links.note: 241 says the wealth among wealths is the wealth of அருள் (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), since goods are found even among the base (பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள). 411 opens with the same formula, செல்வத்துட் செல்வம், and gives the title to what is heard, செவிச்செல்வம். The same superlative is awarded twice, once in the book of virtue and once in the book of statecraft, so a reader sees it is a ranking device applied within a topic, not one fixed doctrine.
links.reason: The formula 'செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்' is awarded to அருட்செல்வம் and to செவிச்செல்வம்; the observation that it is a ranking device is fair.

links.note: 241 separates the two wealths and ranks material wealth low because the base have it too. 757 says அருள், the child borne by அன்பு, is reared by the foster-mother called wealth (பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு). So the book does not let 241 stand as contempt for goods: அருள் ranks higher, yet it needs wealth to grow.
links.reason: 241 ranks 'பொருட்செல்வம்' low ('பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள'), while 757 makes அருள் a child fed by 'பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலி'; a real limit on reading 241 as contempt for goods.

links.note: 241 sets அருட்செல்வம் above பொருட்செல்வம். 914 reuses the pair as அருட்பொருள் and பொருட்பொருளார்: those whose understanding examines the wealth of அருள் (அருட்பொருள் ஆயும் அறிவினவர்) will not touch the cheap charm of women for whom goods are the only wealth. The ranking stated in the abstract in 241 becomes a test of conduct in 914.
links.reason: அருட்செல்வம் over பொருட்செல்வம் in 241 returns as அருட்பொருள் ஆயும் அறிவினவர் against பொருட்பொருளார் in 914. The pair is reused as a test of conduct, as the note says.

links.note: 242 ends பல்லாற்றால் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை: however many ways you examine, அருள் alone is the companion. 132 ends with the same words, தேரினும் அஃதே துணை, said of ஒழுக்கம் (conduct). The identical closing with its exclusive ஏ is given to two different things; read strictly the two claims compete, read as emphasis each chapter is crowning its own subject.
links.reason: Both close with the identical 'தேரினும் அஃதே துணை', said of அருள் in one and ஒழுக்கம் in the other; the note states the competing and the emphatic readings fairly.

links.note: 242 tells one to search by a good path and hold to அருள் (நல்லாற்றான் நாடி அருளாள்க). 324 asks what the good path is (நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின்) and answers: the way that keeps in view not killing anything (யாதொன்றும் கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி). 324 gives content to the நல்லாறு that 242 leaves open, and ties அருள் to not killing.
links.reason: The word நல்லாறு is shared, but in 242 'நல்லாற்றான் நாடி' is the sound way of inquiring (Parimelazhagar: அளவைகளானும் …), not the path of conduct that 324 defines as 'கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி'; so 324 does not fill a gap that 242 leaves open.

links.note: 243 says those whose hearts are joined with அருள் (அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்) do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 5 says the two kinds of deed joined with darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும்) do not join (சேரா) those devoted to the Lord's praise. Both build on சேர், what one is joined to: in 5 darkness is a quality of deeds (Parimelazhagar: மயக்கம்), in 243 it is a place one enters, and joining something else keeps it away.
links.reason: இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் and இருள்சேர் இருவினையும் சேரா share the distinctive இருள்சேர் and the play on சேர் (அருள்சேர்ந்த / பொருள்சேர்). The note's contrast of darkness as place and as quality of deeds is correct.

links.note: 243: no entry into the dark painful world for hearts with அருள். 121: restraint leads among the immortals, lack of restraint drives into thick darkness (அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்). Both use darkness as the destination of a failed virtue, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a hell; 243 states only the exemption, 121 states both directions.
links.reason: 'இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்' and 'ஆரிருள்' are the same image of darkness as the destination, and the note is accurate, but two household virtues with the same afterlife sanction are not different domains; the link is the shared image.

links.note: 244 pairs மன்னுயிர் and தன்னுயிர்: care for other lives frees one's own life from fear. 268 uses the same pair the other way round: one who has fully gained his own life (தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை) is worshipped by all other lives (ஏனைய மன்னுயிரெல்லாம் தொழும்). Together they show the relation running in both directions, from care of others to one's own safety and from self-mastery to others' reverence.
links.reason: The pair மன்னுயிர்/தன்னுயிர் is used in both, in opposite directions: 'மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி ... தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்' and 'தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை ... மன்னுயிரெல்லாந் தொழும்'. The pair recurs elsewhere in the book, so it is less distinctive than the note implies, but the reciprocal reading holds.

links.note: 244: one who tends living beings and holds to அருள் (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி அருளாள்வாற்கு) has no deed his own life need fear (தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்). 326: on the days of one who lives by not killing, Death that eats life does not advance (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று). Both say that sparing other lives secures one's own, once in terms of deeds and once in terms of Death.
links.reason: 'மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி ... தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்' and 'கொல்லாமை ... வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது ... கூற்று' both return protection of other lives to one's own life, as deeds in one and as Death in the other.

links.note: 244 promises that the one who protects lives has nothing his own life need fear. 327 uses the same word, தன்னுயிர், to command not taking another's life even if one's own life goes (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க). 327 shows that the safety promised in 244 is not the condition for the rule: the rule holds even where one's own life is lost.
links.reason: The shared 'தன்னுயிர் ... வினை' wording is real, but 244's 'தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை' is evil deeds the soul dreads (Parimelazhagar: தீவினை, no hell), not a promise of bodily safety, so 327's 'தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும்' does not limit it.

links.note: 245 calls the wide earth where the wind moves a witness (ஞாலம் கரி) that those who hold to அருள் have no distress. 25 calls Indra witness enough (இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி) to the power of one who quenched the five senses. Both close an unprovable claim about a virtue's power by naming a கரி, a witness; 245 appeals to the whole visible world, 25 to one figure from story.
links.reason: Both close on கரி, a witness: மல்லன்மா ஞாலம் கரி and இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி. A distinctive rhetorical device shared meaningfully.

links.note: 245 says flatly that those who hold to அருள் have no distress (அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை), and Parimelazhagar takes this to cover this life. 169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடும்) are to be pondered, which concedes that the upright do meet ruin. The conflict holds if அல்லல் includes worldly ruin and if 169 is read as admitting such cases occur; Parimelazhagar softens 169 with 'if they occur' (உளவாயின்).
links.reason: 245's 'அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை' (Parimelazhagar: இம்மையினும்) and 169's 'செவ்வியான் கேடும்' can rub, and the note states its conditions, but the subjects differ (the compassionate versus the unenvious upright), which the note passes over; the conflict needs them equated.

links.note: 246 says those who leave அருள் and go on doing wrong have, they say, parted from பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்). 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue (அதனை மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு). Both treat wrongdoing as a kind of forgetting; Parimelazhagar reads the பொருள் of 246 as the lasting good, i.e. virtue, which brings the two closer, while Kalaignar reads it as being without wealth.
links.reason: பொச்சாந்தார் and மறத்தல் are both forgetting, but in 246 what is forgotten is unstated (Parimelazhagar: their own suffering; பொருள் is what they 'left', நீங்கி), while 32 is forgetting அறம் itself. The link holds only loosely through Parimelazhagar's பொருள் = அறம், as the note half admits.

links.note: 246 describes the cruel as people who have forgotten (பொச்சாந்தார்); Parimelazhagar says what they forgot is their own suffering. 250 prescribes an act of memory: when going against the weaker, think of yourself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Within the chapter, 250 supplies the remedy for the forgetting that 246 diagnoses.
links.reason: 246's 'பொச்சாந்தார்' (Parimelazhagar: 'தாம் துன்புறுகின்றமையை மறந்தவர்') is answered within the chapter by 250's 'தன்னை நினைக்க'; forgetting and remembering are in the Tamil.

links.note: 247 puts wealth and அருள் in parallel (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி யாங்கு). 248 then breaks the parallel: those without wealth may flower one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished and can hardly become anything again (அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது). The simile of 247 holds for what each lack costs, not for whether the loss can be repaired.
links.reason: 247 sets the two lacks side by side with 'இல்லாகி யாங்கு'; 248 then separates them: 'பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால்' against 'அருளற்றார் அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது'. The note describes both accurately.

links.note: 247 divides the two worlds: this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள். 1042 says the sinner called poverty comes with neither the next life nor this one (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி வரும்). 1042 does not keep the division: poverty costs the next world too, so in the book's later view wealth is not only a this-world matter.
links.reason: 247 assigns only 'இவ்வுலகம்' to wealth, while 1042 says poverty comes with 'மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி', so the neat division does not hold in the poverty chapter.

links.note: 248: loss of wealth can be reversed, loss of அருள் cannot (அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது). 134: even if forgotten, the recited text can be learned again (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்), but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct declines (பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both set a recoverable possession against an unrecoverable loss of character, in the domains of wealth and of learning.
links.reason: 'பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால்' against 'அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது', and 'மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்' against 'பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்': the same recoverable-versus-unrecoverable contrast in wealth and in learning.

links.note: 249 says a virtuous act by one without அருள் is no more reliable than the unclear person's sight of the truth. 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன் ஆகுல நீர பிற). Both place virtue in the inner condition of the doer and discount the outward act that lacks it; 249 names the condition as அருள்.
links.reason: 'அருளாதான் செய்யும் அறம்' discounted, and 'மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன், ஆகுல நீர பிற': both locate virtue in the doer's inner state.

links.note: 249 compares virtue done by one without அருள் to an unclear person seeing the true thing (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்று). 355 defines understanding by the same phrase: seeing the true thing in whatever thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). 355 shows why the comparison in 249 bites: seeing the true thing is what clarity consists in, so without clarity it does not happen, or happens only once by chance as Parimelazhagar reads it (ஒருகால்).
links.reason: 'மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்று' and 'மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு' share the phrase; Parimelazhagar's 'ஒருகால்' is as cited.

links.note: 250 addresses the moment when one has power over a weaker person. 301 says the one who guards anger where it can take effect truly guards it (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்); where it cannot, guarding or not is all one. Both locate the real test of a virtue at the point where one is the stronger party, for அருள் and for anger.
links.reason: மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து and செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் both put the test where one has the upper hand; 301's அல்லிடத்துக் காக்கின் என் makes the point explicit. The same logic in அருள் and in anger.

links.note: 316 gives the general rule: what one has oneself felt to be painful one must not do to another (இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை ... பிறன்கண் செயல்). 250 applies the same use of one's own experience to a difference in strength: recall your own position before the stronger when you stand over the weaker. 250 is the rule of 316 turned into a specific exercise of memory.
links.reason: இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை ... பிறன்கண் செயல் is the general rule from one's own experience, and வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க applies it to the moment of going against மெலியார். A fair application.

links.note: 250 asks one who goes against those weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to think of himself before the stronger, which restrains attacking the weak. 861, with the same words, advises avoiding opposition to the strong and, without holding back, favouring enmity toward the weak (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ஓம்பா மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). The conflict holds on the plain reading of 861 that Pope and Parimelazhagar give; one verse speaks from அருள், the other from a king's choice of enemies. Kalaignar's gloss of 861 as printed here says the opposite (fight the strong, leave the weak), which would remove the conflict but does not match the Tamil.
links.reason: Same vocabulary turned opposite ways: 250 restrains மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து, 861 says ஓம்பா மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை. Note correctly names the reading and the அருள்/statecraft split, and Kalaignar's gloss is indeed inverted as printed.

links.note: 321 asks what virtuous action is and answers not killing (அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை); killing brings all other deeds. 254 uses the same question form for அருள்: what is அருள் and what is not comes down to not killing and killing (யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்). Read together, not killing is the content of both அருள் and virtuous action, which joins the chapter on அருள் to the chapter on not killing. (The first letter of 254 is missing in this edition: ருளல்லது for அருளல்லது.)
links.reason: Both use the frame 'யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்', once for அறவினை and once for அருள்/அல்லது, so non-killing is made the content of both.
links.text_issue: 254 prints ருளல்லது; the initial அ of அருளல்லது is missing.

links.note: 321 makes not killing the answer to what virtuous action is. 297 says that if one keeps up not lying, it is good not to do other virtues (பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). Each verse lets one virtue stand for the whole, and they pick different ones; the conflict holds if both are read as claims of sufficiency and not as chapter emphasis. 323 settles the order inside this chapter by putting not lying second.
links.reason: 'அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை' and 'பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று' each make a different single virtue stand for the whole; the note states the sufficiency reading the conflict depends on and the chapter-emphasis alternative.

links.note: 322 calls sharing one's food and tending many lives (பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல்) the head of all that the authors have gathered. 44 says a household life that fears blame and has shared food (பாத்தூண்) never sees its line fail. Shared eating is the householder's mark in 44; 322 raises the same act to the first place in the chapter on not killing, which Parimelazhagar assigns to renouncers, so the act links the two ways of life.
links.reason: 'பகுத்துண்டு' and 'பாத்தூண்' are the same act of shared eating, a householder's mark in 44 and 'தலை' of all teachings in the non-killing chapter; the note's point about it bridging the two ways of life is fair.

links.note: 322 puts feeding and sustaining lives at the head of the virtues. 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove hunger (அப்பசியை மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்); Parimelazhagar takes the first group to be ascetics. 225 supplies a ranking that fits 322: not harming is completed by actively keeping others alive.
links.reason: 322 makes 'பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல்' the head of virtues; 225 ranks 'பசியை மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றல்' above 'பசி ஆற்றல்', a ranking that fits and extends it. Parimelazhagar's ascetic reading is reported correctly.

links.note: 323 ranks not lying behind not killing. 292 says even falsehood stands in the place of truth if it yields good free of fault (புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்), and Parimelazhagar's example is a false word that saves a life from death. 292 shows the ranking of 323 at work inside the chapter on truth: where truthful speech and a life pull apart, the life decides.
links.reason: 323 puts பொய்யாமை behind கொல்லாமை (பின்சார); 292 lets பொய்மை count as வாய்மை when it yields புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை, and Parimelazhagar's example is a life saved from சாக்காடு.

links.note: 323 says not killing is the one good without equal and not lying is good following behind it (ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை மற்றதன் பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று). 300 says that among all we have seen as true there is nothing at all better than truthfulness (எனைத்தொன்றும் வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற இல்லை). On the literal reading each verse puts a different virtue first; 323 is the only one of the two that states an order between them.
links.reason: ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை with பொய்யாமை பின்சார, against எனைத்தொன்றும் வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற இல்லை. Each puts a different virtue first on the literal reading, as the note says.

links.note: 324: if asked what is called the good path, it is the way that keeps in view not killing anything (யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும் கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி). 291: if asked what is called truth, it is speech with no harm at all in it (யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). The two definitions share their wording, எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும், and both define a positive term by the complete absence of harm, in action and in speech.
links.reason: The shared formula 'எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்' followed by a total negation ('கொல்லாமை', 'தீமை இலாத') is distinctive and the parallel of action and speech is meaningful.

links.note: 325 says that among all who renounced fearing their condition (நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள்), the one who fears killing and keeps not killing in view is chief. 261 defines the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை). 261 states the two parts of the ascetic's practice; 325 says which part decides rank among ascetics.
links.reason: 261 gives two parts of தவம் (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல், உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை); 325 makes கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் the தலை among நீத்தார், so it ranks the second part. Accurate on both.

links.note: 325 ranks the renouncer who keeps to not killing first. 984 says austerity lies in the goodness of not killing (கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை), and sets it beside worth, which lies in not speaking others' faults. The same claim about renouncers appears in the third part of the book of wealth, used there as the measure for a layman's virtue.
links.reason: கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் தலை among நீத்தார், and கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை: the same claim about what austerity consists in, reused in சான்றாண்மை as the model for சால்பு.

links.note: 326 says Death that eats life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 269 says even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) comes within reach of those who have attained the power of austerity. Both give a renouncer's practice power over கூற்று; 269 credits austerity in general, 326 credits the single vow of not killing.
links.reason: 'செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று' and 'கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்' both give a renunciant practice power over personified Death.

links.note: 327 forbids the deed that removes another's life even if one's own life goes (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க). 550 says a king punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. The two conflict if 327 is read as a rule for everyone; Parimelazhagar avoids this by assigning the chapter on not killing to renouncers and 550 to the king's duty.
links.reason: செய்யற்க ... இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை against கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் praised as களைகட்டல். The conflict is real if 327 is universal, and the note states that condition and how Parimelazhagar's ascetic/king division removes it.

links.note: 327: even at the cost of your own life, do not do the deed that takes a life. 656: even if you must see your mother hungry, do not do the deed the worthy condemn (ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க). Both have the form 'even at this extreme cost, செய்யற்க', and both name a வினை as what is forbidden; the first is addressed to the virtuous life, the second to a minister's conduct of affairs.
links.reason: தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க ... வினை and ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க ... வினை have the same 'even at this cost, do not' form in the ascetic's and the minister's domains. Accurate.
links.text_issue: 656 prints 'செய்யற் க' with a stray space.

links.note: 327 puts another's life above one's own. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). In both, one's own life is not the highest value; what outranks it is another creature's life in 327 and one's own sense of shame in 1017.
links.reason: 'தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க' and 'நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்' both place something above one's own life; the note names the two different things accurately.

links.note: 328 says that however great the gain said to bring good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை). Parimelazhagar reads this as the reward promised for killing in sacrifice. 259 says so in its own words: better than a thousand sacrifices with poured oblations is not taking one life and eating (அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின்), which supports that reading of 328 from the text itself.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar reads 'கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம்' as the reward of sacrificial killing, and 259's 'அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின் ... உயிர்செகுத் துண்ணாமை நன்று' ranks sacrifice below not killing in the text itself.

links.note: 328 refuses gain that comes by killing, however great. 311 says that even if one could get wealth that brings distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்), not doing hurt to others is the settled stand of the stainless. The two adjacent chapters make the same refusal for the lesser harm and the greatest one.
links.reason: கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் கடை even when பெரிது, and சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும் பிறர்க்கு இன்னா செய்யாமை: the same refusal of gain through harm, for killing and for lesser hurt in neighbouring chapters.
links.text_issue: 328 prints 'சான்றோர்க் குக்' with a stray space.

links.note: 328: for the worthy (சான்றோர்க்கு), gain got by killing is the lowest (கடை). 657: the utter poverty of the worthy is above gain got with blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவே தலை). Both judge ஆக்கம் by its source from the standpoint of the சான்றோர், with கடை in one and தலை in the other; 328 belongs to the book of virtue and 657 to the conduct of state business.
links.reason: Both judge ஆக்கம் by its source from the standpoint of சான்றோர்: கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் கடை, and கழிநல்குரவே தலை over பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்.

links.note: 329 puts the baseness on those whose work is killing. 256 says that if the world did not kill for the sake of eating, no one would offer flesh for the sake of a price (விலைப்பொருட்டால் ஊன்றருவார் இல்). 256 traces the killer's trade back to those who eat, so the judgment of 329 does not stop at the one who holds the knife.
links.reason: 256 does carry responsibility back to the eaters ('தினற்பொருட்டால் கொல்லாது உலகெனின் ... ஊன்றருவார் இல்'), but 329 never says the baseness stops at 'கொலைவினையர்', so nothing is being limited; this extends the judgment. The commentators also divide on 'கொல்லாது' (Manakkudavar reads it as buying, 'கொள்ளாராயின்'), which the note does not mention.

links.note: 329 treats killers as the settled example of baseness. 551 takes that example as a measure and says a king who takes up harassing his people and does wrong is crueller than those who have taken up killing (கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே). The book of statecraft uses the low point fixed in 329 to rank a bad ruler below it.
links.reason: 329 fixes கொலைவினையர் as புலைவினையர்; 551 uses that floor comparatively: கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே ... வேந்து. Accurate on both.

links.note: 329 says people whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are of base work (புலைவினையர்) in the minds of those who discern baseness. 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs by the difference in the work done (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). Both place a person's standing in what they do; 329 names one occupation and marks it low by the deed, not by birth.
links.reason: 'கொலைவினையர் … புலைவினையர்' assigns lowness by வினை, which is the principle of 'சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்' applied to one case.

links.note: 330 infers a past deed from a present condition: the wretched are those who took life. 37 says there is no need to say 'this is the way of virtue': look between the one who carries the palanquin and the one who rides (சிவிகை பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை). On Pope's and Parimelazhagar's reading both argue from visible fortune back to deeds, 37 for good fortune and 330 for bad; Kalaignar reads 37 differently, as about how the virtuous bear life.
links.reason: 330 reads செயிர் உடம்பின் செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கை back to உயிர் உடம்பின் நீக்கியார், and 37 on the reading named reads சிவிகை பொறுத்தான்/ஊர்ந்தான் back to அறம். The note states which reading it needs and that Kalaignar differs.

links.note: 330 explains diseased and failing lives by past killing. 270 explains why the have-nots are many: those who practise austerity are few and those who do not are many (நோற்பார் சிலர் பலர் நோலாதவர்). Both give a cause in conduct for an unequal condition seen in the world, 330 for individuals and 270 for the proportion in a population.
links.reason: Both explain a visible unequal condition by conduct: 'செயிர் உடம்பின் செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கையவர்' by having taken life, 'இலர் பலராகிய காரணம்' by 'நோலாதவர்' being many. Somewhat general but the explanatory form is shared and the note is accurate.

links.note: 330 says those with afflicted bodies and a failing, evil life (செயிர் உடம்பின் செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கையவர்) are, they say, people who separated life from body. 326 says Death does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. The two verses are the chapter's pair of consequences, both stated in terms of body and lifespan: the non-killer's days are spared and the killer's body and living are spoiled. Parimelazhagar places the killing of 330 in a former birth; the Tamil does not say which birth.
links.reason: Within the chapter, 326's 'வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது ... கூற்று' and 330's 'செயிர் உடம்பின் செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கையவர்' give the paired consequences for the non-killer and the killer; the note rightly says the Tamil does not specify a former birth.

links.note: 381 calls the king who has all six limbs (படை, குடி, கூழ், அமைச்சு, நட்பு, அரண்) 'அரசருள் ஏறு', the male beast among kings; 59 says a man whose home lacks a wife who seeks good name has no 'ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை' before those who scorn him. The same figure of the proud male animal is made to depend on what a man has behind him: a kingdom's six supports in one case, a household's good name in the other. (Parimelazhagar takes ஏறு in 59 as a lion; the word itself only says 'male'.)
links.reason: ஏறு carries the pride in both ('அரசருள் ஏறு', 'ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை'), and in both it depends on what stands behind the man; the note correctly reports Parimelazhagar's lion reading of 59.

links.note: 381 measures a king by possession (ஆறும் உடையான்), and குடி, which Parimelazhagar takes as the land, is one of the six. 740 says a land that has every excellence is still without use (பயமின்றே) if it lacks accord with its ruler (வேந்தமைவு இல்லாத நாடு). Read together, having the limb is not enough: the limb and the king must fit each other.
links.reason: 381 counts குடி among the six the king must உடையான்; 740 says a land with every excellence is பயமின்று if வேந்தமைவு இல்லாத. A real added condition.

links.note: 381 counts the fort (அரண்) among the six things whose possession makes the leading king. 750 says a fort with every excellence (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்) is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The later verse adds the condition that 381's bare 'உடையான்' leaves out.
links.reason: 381 lists 'அரண்' among the six possessions of 'உடையான்'; 750 says 'வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்' however excellent it is, a real condition on bare possession.

links.note: 382 puts அஞ்சாமை first among the king's unfailing qualities. 428 says that not fearing what ought to be feared is folly (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை பேதைமை) and fearing it is the work of the knowing. The king's fearlessness therefore has to be read alongside the அறிவு listed next to it in 382, not as fearing nothing at all.
links.reason: அஞ்சாமை heads the list in 382, and அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை பேதைமை in 428 limits it; அறிவு stands in the same list in 382, as the note says.

links.note: 382 lists fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive (அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவு ஊக்கம்) as a king's nature. 863 describes the man who is easy prey for an enemy: he fears, does not know, does not fit with others, does not give (அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்). Three of the four kingly qualities reappear negated, so the weak enemy of chapter 87 is drawn as the reverse of the king of chapter 39.
links.reason: 'அஞ்சும் அறியான் ... ஈகலான்' negates அஞ்சாமை, அறிவு and ஈகை of 382, three of four as the note counts; the easy enemy is the inverse of the king.

links.note: 383 gives three things that stay with a ruler, beginning with தூங்காமை. 605 gives four that are the pleasure-boat of those bound for ruin: delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep (நெடுநீர் மறவி மடி துயில்). The two lists are near-opposites, and 605 covers both senses the commentators give தூங்காமை in 383 (not delaying, not being slothful).
links.reason: 383's 'தூங்காமை' (Parimelazhagar: விரைவுடைமை; Manakkudavar: மடியின்மை) is negated by 605's 'நெடுநீர் … மடி துயில்'. 'Near-opposite lists' is a slight overstatement, since கல்வி and துணிவு have no counterpart.

links.note: 383 names promptness and resolve (தூங்காமை, துணிவுடைமை) as two separate standing qualities, with learning between them. 668 turns them into one instruction for a single task: once a deed has been seen clearly and decided (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), do it without wavering and with delay driven off (தூக்கம் கடிந்து செயல்). The trait list of the king becomes a sequence: decide, then act at once.
links.reason: தூங்காமை answers தூக்கங் கடிந்து, and துணிவுடைமை (Manakkudavar: ஆராய்ந்து துணிதல்) answers கலங்காது கண்ட வினை. Parimelazhagar takes துணிவு as valour, which the note does not mention, but the sequence reading is defensible.

links.note: 383 says தூங்காமை never leaves those who rule the land; Parimelazhagar reads it as promptness, Manakkudavar as freedom from sloth. 672 uses the same verb in both directions: delay over what should be done with delay (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால), do not delay over what must be done without delay. On Parimelazhagar's reading, 672 limits 383: not-delaying is a rule for some tasks, not all.
links.reason: 383 lists 'தூங்காமை' as a constant royal quality (Parimelazhagar: 'விரைவுடைமை'); 672 says 'தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால'. The note correctly ties the limit to Parimelazhagar's reading and reports Manakkudavar's 'மடியின்மை'.

links.note: 384 makes மானம் part of kingship, on condition that it does not stray from valour (மறன் இழுக்கா மானம்). 432 lists 'மாண்பிறந்த மானம்', honour that has gone past what is fitting, among a ruler's faults. Both verses qualify the same word, so the book's view is that a king's sense of honour is a quality only within bounds.
links.reason: மானம் is a royal quality when 'மறனிழுக்கா' (384) and a royal fault when 'மாண்பிறந்த' (432); the same word bounded from both sides.

links.note: 384 pairs மறன் and மானம் in the king. 766 opens its list of the four safeguards of an army with the same pair (மறம் மானம்), followed by keeping to the proven path and trustworthiness. The same two qualities are required at the top and in the ranks.
links.reason: The pair மறன்/மானம் in 'மறனிழுக்கா மானம்' recurs as 'மறமானம்' heading the army's four safeguards; the king-to-ranks transfer is real.

links.note: 384 asks for honour that does not fall short of valour. 773 says fierceness (தறுகண்) is called great manliness, but helping the foe when something befalls him (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால் ஊராண்மை) is its edge (எஃகு). Parimelazhagar explains 384's phrase with examples of not striking the unequal or the fleeing, which is the restraint 773 states directly.
links.reason: மறனிழுக்கா மானம் is explained by Parimelazhagar with the Chintamani lines on not striking unequal opponents; 773's ஒன்றுற்றக்கால் ஊராண்மை as the எஃகு of பேராண்மை states that restraint outright.

links.note: 385 ends the king's four skills with வகுத்தல், apportioning what has been guarded. 377 uses the same verb for what lies outside human skill: even those who have piled up crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை), which Parimelazhagar takes as fate. The pairing sets the king's apportioning inside a larger one he does not control.
links.reason: வகுத்தல் / வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை share a verb, but the king's allocation of revenue and fate's allotment of enjoyment are different acts; 'sets the king's apportioning inside a larger one' is built on the shared word alone.

links.note: 385 defines the king as able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றல், ஈட்டல், காத்தல், வகுத்தல்). 512 says the man to be given work is one who widens the sources, builds up the yield and looks into what befalls them (வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை ஆராய்வான்). The officer is chosen for the first three of the king's own skills; apportioning is not handed down.
links.reason: 'இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலுங் காத்தலும்' line up with 'வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை ஆராய்வான்'. The remark that வகுத்தல் is not delegated is an argument from silence but is offered as an observation.

links.note: 385 says the king must create ways for wealth to come (இயற்றல்) without naming them. 756 names three that count as the king's wealth: what falls in unowned, customs dues, and what is taken from defeated enemies (உறுபொருள், உல்கு பொருள், ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருள்). Parimelazhagar's note on 385 gives a similar list of sources.
links.reason: 756's 'உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் ... தெறுபொருளும்' fills in what 385's bare 'இயற்றல்' leaves open; Parimelazhagar on 385 does list sources (பகைவரை அழித்தல், திறை கோடல்).

links.note: 386 praises the king who is காட்சிக்கு எளியன், easy to get sight of. 565 says the great wealth of one who is hard to get an audience with and sour-faced (அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான்) is like wealth a ghost has found. Accessibility in 386 earns the land a good name; its absence in 565 makes the king's wealth useless to anyone.
links.reason: 'காட்சிக்கு எளியன் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லன்' is the exact positive of 'அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான்'; the praise and the ghost-wealth verdict state one claim from both sides.

links.note: 386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்), his land is spoken of above others. 566 uses the same word for the reverse case: if he is கடுஞ்சொல்லன் and without kindly regard, his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. One trait is given both its reward and its penalty.
links.reason: The same word 'கடுஞ்சொல்லன்' is negated with a reward in 386 ('மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்') and affirmed with a penalty in 566 ('நெடுஞ்செல்வம் ... ஆங்கே கெடும்'). 'காட்சிக்கெளியன்' and 'கண்ணிலன்' are also near opposites.

links.note: 386 treats ease of access as a quality of a king. 991 says that the practice called courtesy (பண்புடைமை) is easy to reach by being of easy access to everyone (யார்மாட்டும் எண்பதத்தால்). What chapter 39 asks of the ruler, chapter 100 makes the starting point of character for anyone.
links.reason: 'காட்சிக் கெளியன்' for the king and 'எண்பதத்தால் ... யார்மாட்டும்' as the easy road to பண்புடைமை are the same quality in ruler and in anyone.

links.note: 92 ranks the two: being pleasant-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (ஈதலின் நன்றே). 387 does not rank them but joins them, giving 'with' pleasant words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்து), and adds protection. The king's version needs both, where the householder's verse lets speech stand above the gift.
links.reason: 92 ranks 'இன்சொலன் ஆகப் பெறின்' above 'அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதல்'; 387 fuses them in 'இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க'. The note describes both accurately and the contrast between ranking and joining is real.

links.note: 387 says that for one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்து அளிக்க), the world answers to his word. 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layers of kin. The same two means work at two scales: they hold a family around a man and the world around a king.
links.reason: 'இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு' and 'கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்' name the same two means, gathering the world for a king and kin for a man.

links.note: 387's result clause is that the world becomes as the king says and intends (தன் சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து); Manakkudavar reads this as the world lying under his command. 648 says the world quickly takes up the work it is told (விரைந்து தொழில் கேட்கும் ஞாலம்) when it finds those who can speak in order and sweetly. Both make pleasant speech the cause of the world's compliance; 387 adds giving and protection.
links.reason: Both make sweet speech the cause of the world's compliance: 'இன்சொலால் ... தன்சொலால் தான்கண்டனைத்து இவ்வுலகு' and 'விரைந்து தொழில்கேட்கும் ஞாலம் ... இனிது சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்ப் பெறின்'; Manakkudavar's 'தன்னேவலாலே ... தன் வசத்தே கிடக்கும்' is as the note reports.

links.note: 388 says the ruler who does justice and protects is set down as இறை for the people (இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). 50 says the one who lives on earth as one should will be placed among the gods who dwell in heaven (தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). The same passive verb raises a householder by right living and a king by right rule; in both the rank is conferred for conduct. Manakkudavar takes இறை in 388 as 'lord', which would weaken the parallel.
links.reason: Both end 'வைக்கப்படும்': 'இறையென்று' for the just king and 'தெய்வத்துள்' for the right-living householder; the caveat about Manakkudavar's 'நாயகன்' is accurate.

links.note: 388: the king who does முறை and protects is counted as இறை. 547 uses the same two words in a loop: the இறை guards the whole earth, and முறை guards him if he carries it out without fail (அவனை முறை காக்கும்). Justice is what earns the title in 388 and what keeps its holder safe in 547.
links.reason: முறைசெய்து ... இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும் and இறைகாக்கும் ... அவனை முறைகாக்கும் share both key words; justice earns the title in one and guards its holder in the other.

links.note: 388 has the just king set apart as இறை; 702 says one who knows without doubt what is in another's mind should be regarded as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பக் கொளல்). Parimelazhagar glosses both with the same phrase, 'though a man by birth'. The book grants this standing for a function performed, justice in one case and insight in the other.
links.reason: 'இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்' and 'தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பக் கொளல்' both grant divine standing for a function; Parimelazhagar does gloss both with 'மகனேயாயினும்' (388: 'பிறப்பான் மகனேயாயினும்').

links.note: 389 praises a king who endures (பொறுக்கும்) bitter words. 160 says those who fast in penance are great, but rank after those who endure the harsh words others speak (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பார்). Bearing hard speech is rated as the higher discipline for the ascetic and as the quality that holds a kingdom for the king.
links.reason: 'சொற்பொறுக்கும்' and 'இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பார்' do share endurance of hard speech, but 389's words are corrective counsel on Parimelazhagar's reading and 160's are insults; and 160 ranks fasters behind those who bear abuse, so the note's 'higher discipline for the ascetic' misassigns it.

links.note: 389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his support people who rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை). Parimelazhagar reads 389's bitter words as those of exactly such rebuking companions, so 447 gives the institution and 389 the temperament it needs. Manakkudavar reads 389 differently, as hearing of others' offences and bearing it.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar explicitly supplies 'இடிக்கும் துணையாயினார் சொற்கள்' for 389's 'செவிகைப்பச் சொல்', the phrase of 447 ('இடிக்குந் துணையாரை'); the note also reports Manakkudavar's different reading correctly.

links.note: 389 states the king's side: he should bear speech that is bitter to hear. 638 states the minister's side: even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to say what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). The duty to speak does not wait on the king having 389's quality.
links.reason: செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும் is the king's side of bitter counsel, and அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன் is the minister's duty even when the king lacks that quality. Accurate and instructive.

links.note: 390 calls the one who has giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people 'வேந்தர்க்கு ஒளி', a light to kings. 556 uses the same word: kings endure through just rule, and without it 'மன்னர்க்கு ஒளி' does not endure. 390 makes செங்கோல் one of four sources of that light; 556 makes it the one without which the light goes out.
links.reason: 'வேந்தர்க் கொளி' and 'மன்னர்க் கொளி' are the same figure, and செங்கோல்/செங்கோன்மை is one of four sources in 390 and the sole condition in 556; the note reports both accurately.

links.note: 390 lists அளி, kindly care, among the four things a king must have. 557 says what its absence is like: as lack of rain is to the earth, so is the king's lack of அளி to the living (துளியின்மை ... வேந்தன் அளியின்மை). An item in a list becomes, in the chapter on the crooked sceptre, something people cannot live without.
