links.note: 541 gives the steps of justice: examine, favour no one, deliberate, act (ஓர்ந்து ... தேர்ந்து செய்வஃதே முறை). 561 defines the king by the same sequence and adds two things: the punishment must match the offence (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது) and aim at the wrong not recurring (தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்). Chapter 57 thus supplies the measure and purpose that 541 leaves unstated.
links.reason: ஓர்ந்து ... தேர்ந்து செய்வஃதே முறை and தக்காங்கு நாடி share the inquiry, and 561 adds ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது and தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால். Accurate account of what is added.

links.note: 541 makes the refusal of கண்ணோட்டம் part of the definition of முறை. 577 says those without கண்ணோட்டம் have no eyes, and those who have eyes are never without it. If 577 is read without exception, the judge of 541 is 'eyeless' in the moment of judging; the conflict disappears only if 577 is limited to dealings outside judgment, as 578 suggests.
links.reason: 'கண்ணோடாது' is part of முறை in 541, while 577 says 'கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்' without exception; the note states the reading that produces the conflict and the one that removes it.

links.note: 541 defines justice as examining and acting 'யார்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது', letting the eye soften toward no one. 578 says the world belongs to those able to show kindly regard without spoiling the task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு), and Parimelazhagar takes the task to be the king's doing of justice. 578 marks the boundary between the two chapters: regard is welcome up to the point where it would bend the judgment 541 describes.
links.reason: 'கண்ணோடாது … தேர்ந்து செய்வஃதே முறை' is limited by 'கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட'; Parimelazhagar glosses கருமம் as 'முறை செய்தல்' and himself cites 541 there.

links.note: 542: the whole world lives looking to the sky, and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (வானோக்கி ... கோல் நோக்கி). 557 states the same comparison from the side of failure: what lack of rain is to the earth, the king's lack of kindly care is to living beings. The pair shows the rain comparison is about dependence, so that a failed king is a drought.
links.reason: வானோக்கி வாழும் / கோல் நோக்கி வாழும் and துளியின்மை ஞாலத்திற்கு ... வேந்தன் அளியின்மை: the same rain comparison from the positive and the failing side.

links.note: 542 compares subjects' dependence on the sceptre to the world's dependence on rain. In 1192 the woman says the tenderness the loved one gives to the one who loves is like the sky yielding to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்றால்). The same figure of living by the rain is used for a people before their king and a lover before the beloved, and the word அளி serves for both the king's care (557, 390) and the lover's.
links.reason: வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகு / வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்று: the same living-by-rain figure for subjects and for the lover, and அளி does serve for the king's care (557 அளியின்மை).

links.note: 543 makes the sceptre the precondition of scripture and virtue. 19 says that giving and austerity will not last in the wide world if the sky does not give (தானம் தவம் இரண்டும் தங்கா ... வானம் வழங்காதெனின்). Rain in Book 1 and just rule in Book 2 hold the same position: neither is itself virtue, but virtue does not continue without it.
links.reason: The sceptre stands as 'ஆதி' of 'நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும்' and 'தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா ... வானம் வழங்காதெனின்': each is a non-moral precondition without which virtue does not continue.

links.note: 543 speaks of 'அந்தணர் நூல்', which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take as the Veda belonging to Brahmins. 30 defines அந்தணர் as the virtuous (அறவோர்), so called because they live in kindness to every living being. Read with 30, the phrase in 543 can mean the books of the virtuous, which is how Kalaignar takes it; the choice changes what the sceptre is said to uphold.
links.reason: The shared word அந்தணர் is defined in 30 as அறவோர் (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்), which bears directly on அந்தணர் நூல் in 543; the commentators split as the note says (Parimelazhagar/Manakkudavar வேதம், Kalaignar அறவோர் நூல்).

links.note: 543 says the king's sceptre stands as the first ground (ஆதியாய் நின்றது) of the books of the அந்தணர் and of virtue. 560 gives the failing case: if the guardian does not guard, the yield of cows shrinks and those of the six occupations forget their books (அறுதொழிலோர் நூல் மறப்பர்). The claim that learning depends on rule is made once as a principle and once as a consequence.
links.reason: 'அந்தணர் நூற்கும் … ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்' and 'அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர் காவலன் காவான் எனின்' state the dependence of learning on rule as principle and as failure case.

links.note: 544 says the world holds to the king who embraces his people. Parimelazhagar explains the embrace as speaking pleasantly and giving what is needed in hardship, which is what 387 names: to one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க), this world answers. 387 says how the embrace is done; 544 adds that it goes together with the sceptre.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does explain 'குடிதழீஇ' as 'இன்சொல் சொல்லுதலும், தளர்ந்துழி வேண்டுவன கொடுத்தலும்', which is 387's 'இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க', and both end with the world's adherence ('அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு'). The identification rests on the commentator, as the note says.

links.note: 544: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும்) of the king who embraces his people (குடிதழீஇ) while wielding the sceptre. 1025: the world gathers round as kin (சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு) the man who raises his family and lives without fault. In both the world's attachment is the return for care of one's own குடி, the word meaning the king's subjects in 544 and a man's family in 1025.
links.reason: 'குடிதழீஇ ... அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு' and 'குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச் சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு' both make the world's attachment the return for care of one's குடி, subjects in one and family in the other.

links.note: 545 ties rain to the king's right rule. 55 ties it to a wife's fidelity: she who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain' and it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). In the household and in the kingdom the book makes rain answer to a person keeping to their proper role.
links.reason: 'கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட பெயலும்' and 'பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை' both make rain answer to a person keeping their role, in kingdom and in household.

links.note: 545 says harvest (விளையுள்) comes with just rule. 239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). Both let the moral state of people show in the fertility of the land; 239 does it for any person, 545 for the king.
links.reason: 'பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு' under a just king and 'வண்பயன் குன்றும் இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்' both let human moral standing show in the land's yield.

links.note: 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be (இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும்). 559: if the king acts bending justice (முறைகோடி), the sky bends its showers and does not rain (உறைகோடி). The two verses state one causal claim in both directions, and 559 echoes the bent sceptre in the bent rain.
links.reason: 'இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் ... பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு' and 'முறைகோடி ... உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்' state the same rule-and-rain causality in both directions.

links.note: 546's condition is that the கோல் does not bend (கோடாது). 118 praises not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like the கோல், here the balance beam, that first levels itself and then weighs. The same word and the same verb serve for the king's sceptre and the scales, so the straightness asked of the ruler is the impartiality asked of the worthy in Book 1.
links.reason: கோல் ... கோடாது of the sceptre and கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை of the balance: same noun and verb for royal justice and personal impartiality.

links.note: 546 sets spear against sceptre: it is not the வேல் that gives victory but the king's கோல், if it does not bend. 552 uses the same pair to opposite effect: the demand of one who stands with a கோல் is like one standing with a வேல் and saying 'hand it over'. The sceptre is better than the spear only while straight; bent toward extortion, 552 says it is the spear.
links.reason: வேல் and கோல் are paired in both: வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது ... கோல் when கோடாது, and கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு likened to வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது. A distinctive shared pair used to opposite effect.

links.note: 547: the king guards the earth, and justice guards the king (இறை காக்கும் ... முறை காக்கும்). 57: what can the guard of confinement do? The guard that women keep by their own steadfastness is the chief guard (சிறை காக்கும் காப்பு ... நிறை காக்கும் காப்பே தலை). Both verses, in the same rhyming pattern, say that real protection comes from the guarded person's own conduct and not from outside force.
links.reason: இறைகாக்கும் ... முறைகாக்கும் and சிறைகாக்கும் ... நிறைகாக்கும் match in rhyme and in logic: what truly guards is the person's own முறை or நிறை. 'Not from outside force' is explicit only in 57, a small overstatement for 547.

links.note: 547 says justice protects the king if he does it without fail. 448 calls the king who has no one to rebuke him 'ஏமரா மன்னன்', a king without a guard, and says he perishes even with no one to ruin him. Together they name what guards a ruler: his own just practice and the people who correct him.
links.reason: 'அவனை முறைகாக்கும்' and 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்' (ஏமம் = guard) both name what protects the protector; pairing just practice with rebuking counsellors is instructive.

links.note: 548: a king who is not easy of access (எண்பதத்தான் in the negative, as Parimelazhagar construes it) and does not examine and do justice sinks and perishes. 386: a king easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh in speech has his land praised. Accessibility is stated as a virtue in chapter 39 and its lack as a cause of ruin in chapter 55.
links.reason: 'எண்பதத்தான்' (taken in the negative, as Parimelazhagar explains) and 'காட்சிக்கு எளியன்' state accessibility as a cause of ruin when absent and of praise when present.

links.note: 548 says the unjust, unapproachable king perishes of himself (தானே கெடும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even without enemies'. 448 says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes though no one sets out to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe a ruler's fall with no outside agent, caused by shutting out complaint in one case and criticism in the other.
links.reason: தானே கெடும் and கெடுப்பாரிலானும் கெடும்: a ruler ruined with no outside agent, by refusing access/justice in one and rebuke (இடிப்பார்) in the other.

links.note: 548 and 553 share most of a line: a king who does not examine and do justice (ஓரா / நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்). In 548 the king himself perishes; in 553 he loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The pairing shows the same neglect ruining the ruler and the country.
links.reason: 'ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்' and 'நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்' are the same subject, with 'தானே கெடும்' in one and 'நாடு கெடும்' in the other; ruler and country ruined by the same neglect.

links.note: 314 tells a person how to punish those who hurt him: shame them by doing them good and let it go (அவர் நாண நன்னயம் செய்து விடல்). 549 says that for a king, guarding the people and removing offences (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). The words 'no stain' answer the doubt that punishing goes against virtue, which Parimelazhagar spells out; 549 limits 314's rule to one's own injuries and exempts the office.
links.reason: 314's ஒறுத்தல் by 'நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்' against 549's 'குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்'; Parimelazhagar does raise and answer the doubt that punishing is a stain, as the note says.

links.note: 549 makes removing offences the king's work. 436 sets an order for it: if he first removes his own fault and then looks at others' (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றம் காண்கிற்பின்), what fault can attach to a ruler? The right to punish in 549 is, by 436, clear of blame only for a king who has corrected himself first.
links.reason: 549's 'குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று' is conditioned by 436's order 'தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின் என்குற்றமாகும் இறைக்கு'.

links.note: 549 clears the punishing king of blame. 567 says harsh words and punishment that goes beyond bounds (கையிகந்த தண்டம்) are a file that wears down a king's strength to defeat enemies. Punishment is the king's work only within measure; past it, the same act damages him.
links.reason: 549: குற்றம் கடிதல் வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்; 567: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is the அரம் that wears down his அடுமுரண். A clean limit of measure on the first.

links.note: 550 justifies the king's use of death against the cruel (கொடியார்). 551 turns the same words on the king: one who takes up harassing his people and does wrong is crueller than those who have taken up murder (கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே). Placed on either side of the chapter break, the two verses make the king both the one who removes the cruel and the one who can be the worst of them.
links.reason: கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் and கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே ... வேந்து reuse கொலை/கொடி/வேந்து across the chapter boundary, turning the measure onto the king himself.

links.note: 550 compares the king's execution of the cruel to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). 1038, on farming itself, says that after weeding (கட்டபின்) guarding the crop is better than watering it. In the farmer's own chapter weeding is one step and guarding counts for more, which fits 549's order of guarding the people first and punishing second.
links.reason: The weeding figure is shared ('பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு' / 'கட்டபின்'), but 1038 ranks காப்பு above நீர், not above weeding, so the note's claim that guarding outranks weeding and mirrors 549's order is not in the verse.

links.note: 483 asks whether anything called அருவினை exists for one who acts with கருவி and knowing காலம். 631 uses the same three words but keeps அருவினை as a separate item the minister must be good at. The pair shows where the minister's list comes from: tools and timing are what make a hard task doable.
links.reason: கருவி, காலம் and அருவினை appear in both; 483's rhetorical 'அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ' explains why the minister's list in 631 holds these items together.

links.note: 631 defines the minister as one excellent in கருவி, காலம், செய்கை and the அருவினை itself. 675 turns nearly the same list into a rule for anyone acting: பொருள், கருவி, காலம், வினை, இடன், 'ஐந்தும் இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்'. Read together, the minister's defining competence is the checklist of 675, with resources and place added there.
links.reason: கருவி, காலம், செய்கை/வினை appear in both lists; 675 adds பொருள் and இடன் and turns the list into a rule (இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்). The note describes both correctly.

links.note: 632 lists the minister's qualities: வன்கண், குடிகாத்தல், கற்றறிதல், ஆள்வினை. 382 lists the king's: அஞ்சாமை, ஈகை, அறிவு, ஊக்கம் (383 adds கல்வி and துணிவுடைமை). Firmness, knowledge and drive appear on both lists, so the minister is described on the king's pattern; Manakkudavar even glosses வன்கண் as அஞ்சாமை. Giving is on the king's list only.
links.reason: 'வன்கண் ... கற்றறிதல் ஆள்வினை' line up with 'அஞ்சாமை ... அறிவு ஊக்கம்', and Manakkudavar does gloss வன்கண் as அஞ்சாமை; the note also correctly marks ஈகை as the king's alone.

links.note: 187 says those who cannot make friends with pleasant talk 'கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்', split even their own kin, by divisive speech. 633 uses the same verb, பிரித்தல், for a minister's skill, which Parimelazhagar restricts to detaching an enemy's allies. The same act is a fault at home and a craft in statecraft, and what differs is whose bond is being broken.
links.reason: கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் in 187 and பிரித்தல் in 633 are the same act, a fault among one's own and a skill against an enemy's allies (Parimelazhagar's restriction is correctly reported). The contrast teaches something.

links.note: 633 names rejoining those who parted as a minister's skill. 530 says how the king should handle such a return: one who left (உழைப்பிரிந்து) and came back for a reason is to be taken in after thought, 'எண்ணிக் கொளல்'. The pair shows that பொருத்தல் is not unconditional welcome; 530 supplies the caution.
links.reason: 'பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்' as a skill meets 'உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை … எண்ணிக் கொளல்', which adds deliberation before taking the returner in.

links.note: 633 says a minister must be able to divide (பிரித்தல்), keep his own side (பேணிக் கொளல்) and rejoin those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 679 ranks one such act: 'ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்', bringing the unattached over, is more urgent than doing good to friends. 679 gives a priority among the alliance skills that 633 only lists.
links.reason: 679 does rank alliance-making above 'நட்டார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்', but 'ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்' is about foes (or the foe's foes, per Parimelazhagar), not 633's 'பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்'; the note's 'unattached' and 'one such act' blur that.

links.note: 462 tells the one acting that nothing is out of reach if he examines with a chosen circle and thinks it over himself: 'தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு'. 634 describes the minister with the same two verbs, தெரிதல் and தேர்ந்து செயல். The pairing shows the two sides of one arrangement: 462 is the ruler's need for such company, 634 is what that company must be able to do.
links.reason: Both verses use the roots தெரி and தேர் (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி / தெரிதலும் தேர்ந்து செயலும்); 462's 'chosen company' is plausibly the ministerial circle whose abilities 634 lists. In 462 தெரிந்த means 'chosen', a small looseness in 'same two verbs'.

links.note: 634 asks of a minister தெரிதல், தேர்ந்து செயல் and 'ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல்', speaking so that the matter is settled. 671 says 'சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்': deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and letting that resolve linger is a fault. Parimelazhagar glosses ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல் as speaking so that துணிவு arises, which makes the minister's decisive word the point where 671's deliberation closes.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does gloss 'ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல்' as speaking so that 'துணிவு பிறக்கும் வகை', which matches 671's 'சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்'. His gloss is narrower (about dividing or uniting others) than the note suggests, but ஒருதலை itself supports the link.

links.note: 441 tells the king to choose the friendship of those who are 'அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார்', 'திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து'. 635 describes the counsel-companion in the same words: 'அறனறிந்து ... திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை'. 441 is the instruction to seek such a person and 635 is the portrait of him, with settled speech (ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்) added.
links.reason: The shared 'அறனறிந்து … திறனறிந்து … தேர்' vocabulary links the instruction to choose such men (441) with the portrait of the 'தேர்ச்சித் துணை' (635).

links.note: 635 asks for one who knows அறன், has full and settled speech, and knows திறன். 644 joins the same three terms in one rule: 'திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை', since no அறன் or பொருள் is beyond that. The next chapter thus takes the speech item of 635 and makes fitted speech itself the place where knowing virtue and knowing method show.
links.reason: அறன், சொல், திறனறிந்து do recur, but திறன் in 635 is the minister's knowledge of how to act and in 644 it is fitting speech to the hearer, and 644 says only that no அறன் or பொருள் exceeds such speech. The claim that fitted speech is 'where knowing virtue and method show' goes beyond the Tamil.

links.note: 636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have மதிநுட்பம் together with நூல். 373 says that however many subtle books one studies (நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும்), one's own உண்மை அறிவு still prevails. 373 explains why 636 puts native subtlety first and adds books 'ஓடு': study does not replace the native intelligence, so the combination is not open to everyone who reads. Parimelazhagar ties 373's native understanding to ஊழ்.
links.reason: மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு in 636 and நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் ... உண்மையறிவே மிகும் in 373 both rank native understanding against book learning, and 373 does limit what நூல் alone can supply. Note's commentary citation is accurate.

links.note: 636 implies that nothing withstands the person who has native subtlety and learning. 503 says that even in those who have studied hard texts and are free of fault (அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார்), close examination rarely finds no blankness: 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு'. The praise in 636 concerns outwitting opposing schemes; 503 limits it, since the learned still have gaps.
links.reason: 636's rhetorical 'யாவுள முன்நிற்பவை' praises wit plus learning against opposing schemes, while 503's 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு' is about residual ignorance found when vetting; they touch the limits of learning but 503 does not really condition 636's claim.

links.note: 637 says that even when one knows the செயற்கை, which Parimelazhagar takes as the method taught in treatises, one should act knowing the உலகத்து இயற்கை. 140, in the chapter on conduct, says those who have not learned 'உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்' are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). The same ranking of learning below fit with the world appears once for personal conduct and once for a minister's action.
links.reason: உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல் even after knowing செயற்கை; உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் கல்லார் are அறிவிலாதார் though பலகற்றும். Same ranking in a minister's action and in personal conduct.

links.note: 426 defines அறிவு as living with the world in the way the world lives: 'உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது'. 637 gives the working form of this for one who already knows the method: 'உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்'. Together they treat attention to how the world actually goes as part of knowledge and not a concession against it.
links.reason: 'உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்' and 'உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது அறிவு' both make conformity to how the world goes part of knowing, for the minister and as a definition of அறிவு.

links.note: 638 makes it the duty (கடன்) of the one at the king's side to say what is sound (உறுதி) even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself. 448 gives the stake: a king without those who rebuke, 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்', perishes even with no one to ruin him. 448 shows why 638 does not release the minister when the king will not listen.
links.reason: 'உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்' even to an 'அறிகொன்று அறியான்' is explained by the stake in 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத … கெடும்'.

links.note: 638 obliges the minister to speak sound counsel regardless of the king's reception. 696 governs the manner: knowing the king's mood and considering the time, say what is needed without what is disliked, so that it is wanted ('வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்'). The duty of 638 stands, and 696 conditions how and when it is discharged.
links.reason: 638 makes 'உறுதி கூறல்' a 'கடன்' whatever the king's reception; 696 conditions the delivery with 'குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்'. A genuine qualification of manner, not of the duty.

links.note: 849 says 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்': one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up not seeing himself, while the other keeps to what he saw. 638 requires exactly this of a minister when the king 'அறிகொன்று அறியான்'. The conflict holds if 849 is read as general advice not to instruct the conceited; Parimelazhagar reads it as a report that the instructor is reviled, which would leave 638 as a duty carried at that cost.
links.reason: 'அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் … கூறல் கடன்' requires what 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்' says rebounds on the instructor; the note states which reading makes it a conflict and gives Parimelazhagar's 'பழிக்கப்பட்டு' reading correctly.

links.note: 639 and 817 use the same construction and the same kind of figure: 'மந்திரியின் ... எழுபது கோடி உறும்' and 'நட்பின் பகைவரால் பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்'. In both an inflated count of open enemies is set against one false intimate, a plotting minister in 639 and a friend good only for laughter in 817. Parimelazhagar reads உறும் in 639 as 'that many enemies will come', and notes others read it as 'that many times better', which is how 817 is read.

links.note: 1090 says brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it and does not, like love, gladden those who merely see ('கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல்'). 1092 puts a measure on that: the small look her eyes steal ('கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்') is not an even half of love but more ('செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது'). Together they make sight alone a large share of love's pleasure; Parimelazhagar takes the 'half' in 1092 to be half of physical union.
links.reason: கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் in 1090 makes sight a source of love's pleasure, and 1092 measures it: சிறுநோக்கம் is காமத்தில் செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது. Adjacent chapters, a real step from one to the other.

links.reason: சிறுநோக்கம் ... செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது and புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது do both place love's larger share outside union, but both are in the same domain (காமம்), so this is two verses making a similar claim, not a pattern carried into another domain.

Both use watering for a sign or word given to someone already receptive: the gesture or speech does not start the growth, it feeds it.

In 1147 the woman says her sickness grows long with the town's gossip as manure and her mother's words as water ('அன்னைசொல் நீராக நீளும் இந்நோய்'). The same cultivation figure serves first for what encourages love and later for what, meant to check it, only makes its pain grow.

links.note: In 1094 she looks at the ground when he looks at her ('நிலன்நோக்கும்') and looks at him and smiles when he does not. In 1114 the blue lilies, if they could see, would bend and look at the ground ('கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்') because they cannot match her eyes. The identical phrase marks shyness in the first verse and conceded defeat in the second; Parimelazhagar glosses both as bowing from நாண்.
links.reason: The identical 'நிலன்நோக்கும்' is the girl's shyness in 1094 and the lilies' bowed defeat in 1114; Parimelazhagar attributes both to நாண் (1094 heading, 'அந்நாணினால்' in 1114).

links.note: 1096: though they speak like those unattached ('உறாஅதவர்போல் சொலினும்'), the words of those without anger are quickly understood ('செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). 826 has the same frame reversed: though they say good things like friends ('நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும்'), the words of the unreconciled are quickly understood ('ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). The shared wording shows one claim applied in love and in statecraft: a spoken mask, harsh or kind, does not long hide the disposition behind it.
links.reason: The frames are nearly identical: '...போல் சொலினும் செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்' and 'நட்டார்போல் ... சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்', reversed between love and false friendship.

links.note: 709 says the eye itself tells enmity and friendship, if one has people who understand the eye's kinds ('கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்'). 1097 is a case that needs that skill: here a look like an enemy's is a mark of closeness, not of enmity. The pairing shows why 709 adds its condition; a hostile look cannot be taken at face value.
links.reason: 709 conditions the eye's testimony on கண்ணின் வகைமை உணர்வார்; 1097's செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும் as உற்றார் குறிப்பு is exactly a look that misleads without that skill. Both sit in chapters titled குறிப்பறிதல்.

links.note: 1097 lists small harsh words spoken without anger and looks like an enemy's ('செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்') as the signs of those who are close while seeming distant. 824 warns of the opposite pairing: a sweet smile on the face with bitterness inside ('முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா'). In both the surface is the reverse of the heart; the lover reads the mismatch with relief, the Book of Wealth reads it with fear.
links.reason: 'செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும் ... உறாஅர்போன்று உற்றார்' and 'முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா' are mirror cases of surface reversing heart, read with relief in one book and fear in the other.

links.note: In 1098, when he looks she softens and smiles gently ('பசையினள் பைய நகும்'), and he says there is a certain grace in her then ('உண்டு ஆண்டு ஓர் ஏஎர்'). 1274 says there is something inside the bud of her smile, like scent inside a closed bud ('நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன்று உண்டு'). Both treat her slight smile as holding an unspoken meaning, and both leave that meaning as an unnamed 'something'.
links.reason: Both find an unnamed 'something' in her slight smile, each with உண்டு: 'உண்டாண்டோர் ஏஎர் ... பைய நகும்' and 'நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன் றுண்டு'.

links.note: 1099 says looking at each other with the common look, like strangers ('ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்'), is found in lovers. 528 uses the same word for a king: he should not look on all in common ('பொதுநோக்கான்') but by rank, and many will live looking to that. In 528 the undifferentiated look is a failure to distinguish; in 1099 it is put on deliberately by the two people who distinguish each other most.
links.reason: பொதுநோக்கு is a rare shared term: lovers put it on (ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்) and a king should not look that way (பொதுநோக்கான் ... வரிசையா நோக்கின்). The note reads both correctly and the contrast is meaningful.

links.note: 1100: when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words are of no use at all ('வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல'). 705, in the Book of Wealth's chapter of the same name, asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign ('என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்'). Both hold that the eye is the organ for knowing another's mind; 705 says so for court service and 1100 for lovers, where it makes speech redundant.
links.reason: Both verses of same-named chapters turn on 'என்ன பயன்': eyes useless if they cannot read 'குறிப்பிற் குறிப்பு', words useless once 'நோக்கொக்கின்'. The eye as the organ of knowing another's mind appears in court and in love.

links.note: 1100 says that once the eyes agree, words from the mouth serve no purpose. 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading ('கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு') adds womanhood to womanhood. 1280 moves from the fact that eyes can replace speech to praise of the woman who chooses to speak that way.

links.note: 1151 tells him to announce his quick return to those who will be alive then ('வாழ்வார்க்கு உரை'), implying she will not be. 1160 says many consent to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads this as her ironic reply to the friend, meaning she is not one of them. The chapter opens and closes on the same word, 'வாழ்வார்', for the survivors she sets herself apart from.

In 1263 the woman, after he has gone, says she is still alive through wanting his return ('வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்'). The later speech shows the claim of 1151 as said in the moment: the hope of return that was dismissed there is what keeps her alive here.

Both quote the same promise back and place the blame or shame on the one who broke it, not on her.

Both reject return as a remedy and allow only not-leaving; Parimelazhagar supplies that what is to be protected in 1155 is her life.

The hardness she charges him with before parting she later charges to herself, or to women like her, for surviving it.

In 1222 she asks the evening, which looks as wretched as she is, whether its partner too is hard like hers ('எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ'). The epithet given conditionally in 1156 has become her settled description of him once he is gone.

links.note: In 1157 the slipping bangles broadcast ('தூற்றா') his leaving. In 1235 the shoulders that have lost bangles and their old beauty tell of the cruel one's cruelty ('கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்'). Both make her thinning body a speaker that reports on him without her consent; 1235 adds a judgment of him to the bare news of 1157.

links.note: 1157 asks whether the bangles slipping past her wrist do not proclaim that the man of the shore has left her ('துறைவன் துறந்தமை தூற்றாகொல்'). 1277 says the bangles understood before she did that the man of the cool shore had parted ('தணந்தமை நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை'). Same man, same ornament: in 1157 the bangles tell others, in 1277 they know ahead of her, which Parimelazhagar takes as his parting in mind while still present.
links.reason: The same 'துறைவன்' and the same 'வளை': in 1157 the bangles 'தூற்றாகொல்' his leaving to others, in 1277 they 'நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த' it. Distinctive shared image, accurately described.

links.note: 1158: living in a town without one's own people is painful, and parting from one who is dear is more painful still ('அதனினும் இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு'). 839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting brings no pain at all ('பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்று இல்'). Read together, both verses use the pain of parting as the measure of what a bond was worth: none for a fool's friendship, more than exile among strangers for a lover.
links.reason: 'அதனினும் இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு' and the ironic 'பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்' both measure a bond by what parting costs; the note marks the irony and that this is a joint reading.

links.note: 1159 asks whether fire, which burns when touched, can burn when one lets go as love's sickness does ('விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ'). 1104 has the man ask where she got a fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near ('நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும்'). The same reversed fire is a marvel in the man's mouth at union and a complaint in the woman's (for Parimelazhagar) at parting.
links.reason: The same reversed fire: 'விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ' and 'நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ', a wonder at union and a complaint at parting.

links.note: 1160 says many agree to the hard thing, put away their pain, endure the parting and live on ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads it as irony against the friend's advice. 1198 says outright that none in the world are harder than those who live on ('வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்') without a kind word from the beloved. Both treat surviving separation as something that needs explaining, not as the expected course.
links.reason: Parimelazhagar does read 'பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்' as implying that no one does so ('குறிப்பால் தோன்ற'), and 1198 says 'வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்'; both treat living on after separation as the abnormal case. The agreement depends on the ironic reading of 1160, which the note flags.
